text: Before comparing simulated motion with theory, we need a measure of how far the represented value moves. Let $x(t)$ be that value at absolute time $t$, and let $\ell$ be the time between two observations, called the lag. [The [**displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)$.]{.definition-explanation} The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the average of $(\Delta x)^2$ over intervals with the same lag. The average can use different starting times along a recording, repeated trials, or both; which intervals can be combined depends on whether their movement statistics are comparable. Squaring prevents leftward and rightward changes from cancelling.

text: Noise generally puts $\mathbf s$ slightly away from the attractor. To assign it a memory coordinate, imagine turning off further noise and following the deterministic return flow. [The fixed point reached by this flow is the paper's [**instantaneous attractor state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}; $\theta$ labels that point.]{.definition-explanation} This local definition assumes that nearby states return to a unique point on the continuous family. It uses the circuit's return dynamics, which can differ from a perpendicular geometric projection. [Original definition and Figure 1A, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2).

text: **Neural mechanism.** The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. Burak and Fiete give this physical interpretation: maintaining the state acts like estimating it again from roughly one synaptic time constant $\tau$ of the network's own spikes. For a state held fixed, that sample would supply information $J\tau$, so even an ideal locally unbiased estimate would have variance at least $1/(J\tau)$. Comparing this with the variance $2D\tau$ accumulated over the same time suggests $2D\tau\ge1/(J\tau)$. One factor of $\tau$ comes from collecting information; the other comes from accumulating displacement variance. This is the paper's heuristic interpretation; the proof below establishes the inequality from the projection assumptions. [Paper interpretation, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3).

[A [**systematic drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a nonzero mean velocity.]{.definition-explanation} The eye paper's term “fixational drift” names the eye's slow motion between saccades, which can be largely random; it does not imply a nonzero mean velocity.

We begin by following the distribution of stored values across repeated trials, using the local diffusion coefficient derived in the preceding chapter. This shows why errors can keep growing on a line but level off when angular error is measured within one turn. We then separate random spreading from systematic drift and make the noise assumptions explicit. Finally, the paper's figures show what its network simulations test and distinguish movement of the memory from uncertainty when another circuit reads it. That second uncertainty motivates the information calculation that follows.
